newsitem.title: CROATIA: Croat Pliva sees growth boosting profit.
newsitem.headline: Croat Pliva sees growth boosting profit.

text.p: Croatia's leading drugs firm Pliva on Friday announced a 14.4-percent increase in the 1996 net profit to 456 million kuna ($84 million), and foresaw its planned growth further boosting profits this year.
"We hope to ensure a larger net profit for our shareholders than last year," company president Zeljko Covic told a news conference, but declined to give a precise figure.
He said Pliva aimed to continue expanding the sales and exports in particular, seeing central and eastern Europe as the key target market in the future:
"We expect very strong growth rates in this market."

Pliva's 1996 net per share earnings rose to 861 kuna, or five percent from a year earlier, Covic said. He added that its equity had since then received a boost of 222 million kuna or 30 percent from the stock sale and retained profit.
The company is proposing a per share dividend of 248 kuna for 1996, compared to the 235 kuna paid on 1995 results. Its annual shareholders' meeting is set for June 20.
Pliva's ordinary stock were split 37-for-1 and reissued with a face value of 100 kuna each in January this year.
Its shares gained six kuna on Friday to close at 485 on the Zagreb bourse on the back of these news and traders saw them likely to fuel Pliva's steady price rise next week.
However, its 1/5 Global Depositary Receipts listed in London, fell back to $15.85 from $16.2 each since the profits were announced earlier in the day.
It was the first Croatian company to get a listing on the London Stock Exchange in April last year.
Pliva reported a pre-tax profit of 616 million kuna ($113 million) for 1996 after a 30.9 percent annual increase due to better sales, royalties income and considerable cost reduction.
Its total income rose 9.4 percent to 2.27 billion kuna ($418 million), and was mostly accounted for by sales.
The share of exports widened to 45.6 percent of the total after booming 17.7 percent last year from 1995, the company said in its 1996 report.

Covic put the overall sales rise at 50 percent in the past four years as Pliva recovered from a drastic slump caused by the 1991 war in Croatia. He gave last year's foreign sales income as $188 million, compared to $135 million in 1993.
Apart from pharmaceuticals, of which its strategic drug azithromycin is the most famous and important worldwide, Pliva also exports some food products. It hopes all will attract more buyers abroad.
"The only product we may not be increase (the sale of) this year is azithromycin," Covic said, blaming this on production constrictions.
But the company counts on opening a new plant for the key drug near Zagreb in 1998 to enable a future boost, he added.

Azithromycin is marketed under licence by Pfizer as Zithromax in the United States and Western Europe. Covic said it recorded the fastest growth of all antibiotics in the U.S. in 1996, after being approved for paediatric care.
Among other markets that performed well last year, he also mentioned the former Eastern bloc except Russia, which had a shortfall, and China.
Covic put total 1996 investments into new production lines, research and development at 320 million kuna. Pliva is currently developing 60 new chemical entities.
"If we want to ensure a stable growth for the 21st century, we have to invest vast sums of money into research," he said.
